```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

# Female wood frogs from breeding ponds along an urbanization gradient in
# Baltimore County, MD (Jennette et al. 2019)
wood_frogs <- read_csv("../data/female-wood-frogs.csv") |>
  mutate(
    habitat = factor(
      str_to_title(POP),
      levels = c("Rural", "Suburban", "Urban")
    )
  ) |>
  select(habitat, svl = SVL, age = Age)


pop_colours <- c(
  Rural = "forestgreen",
  Suburban = "goldenrod",
  Urban = "grey40"
)

# Residual sum of squares
rss <- function(m) sum(residuals(m)^2)

# Points by group, with each observation's residual drawn to the fitted value.
# Fixed seed so the jitter matches when comparing two models side by side.
plot_residuals <- function(frogs, model, title) {
  set.seed(222)
  frogs |>
    mutate(
      fit = fitted(model),
      x = as.numeric(habitat) + runif(n(), -0.2, 0.2)
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, svl)) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = fit), colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(aes(fill = habitat), shape = 21, size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(x = x - 0.3, xend = x + 0.3, y = fit, yend = fit),
      frogs |>
        mutate(fit = fitted(model)) |>
        distinct(habitat, fit) |>
        mutate(x = as.numeric(habitat)),
      linewidth = 1.5
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(levels(frogs$habitat)),
      labels = levels(frogs$habitat)
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pop_colours, guide = "none") +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "SVL (mm)",
      title = title,
      subtitle = sprintf("RSS = %.1f", rss(model))
    )
}
```

# ANOVA

## Learning objectives

- **Review** categorical predictors
- **Compute** degrees of freedom from data and model
- **Compare** simpler and more complex models

## Are urban frogs smaller?

Cities build stormwater ponds to manage runoff. Amphibians breed in them. But are they _good_ habitat?

Jennette et al. (2019) measured female wood frogs breeding in rural, suburban, and urban ponds.

- **Snout-vent length (SVL)**: body length in mm, a measure of size
- **Age**: years, estimated from growth rings in toe bones

Smaller frogs lay fewer eggs, so if urban frogs are smaller _at the same age_, urban habitat may be lower quality.

## Meet the wood frogs

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(wood_frogs, aes(habitat, svl, fill = habitat)) +
  geom_jitter(shape = 21, size = 3, width = 0.15, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pop_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "SVL (mm)",
    title = sprintf("Female wood frogs (n = %d)", nrow(wood_frogs))
  )
```

# Review categorical predictors

## Dummy variables

Category levels are text. You can't multiply a coefficient by a word.

So we use **dummy variables**: one level becomes the **reference**, every other level gets a 0/1 variable.

::: {.columns style="font-size:0.8em"}

::: {.column}

| Habitat | Suburban | Urban |
|------------|:--------:|:-----:|
| Rural      | 0        | 0     |
| Suburban   | 1        | 0     |
| Urban      | 0        | 1     |

:::

::: {.column}

$k$ levels get $k - 1$ dummy variables

Here: 3 levels, 2 dummies. Rural is the reference.

:::

:::

## Three categories: equation

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
$$
\begin{align}
\text{SVL} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{Habitat} = \text{Suburban}) \\
&\quad + \beta_2 (\text{Habitat} = \text{Urban}) + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
$$
:::

| Habitat | Expected SVL |
|------------|-----------|
| Rural      | $\beta_0$ |
| Suburban   | $\beta_0 + \beta_1$ |
| Urban      | $\beta_0 + \beta_2$ |

## Three categories: visual

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center

three_lm <- lm(svl ~ habitat, wood_frogs)
three_means <- tibble(
  habitat = factor(
    levels(wood_frogs$habitat),
    levels = levels(wood_frogs$habitat)
  )
) |>
  mutate(svl = predict(three_lm, newdata = pick(everything())))
ref_mean <- three_means$svl[1]

ggplot(wood_frogs, aes(habitat, svl)) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(fill = habitat),
    shape = 21,
    size = 3,
    width = 0.15,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ref_mean, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = habitat, y = ref_mean, yend = svl),
    three_means[-1, ],
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(data = three_means, size = 5, shape = "diamond") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.6,
    y = ref_mean + 0.6,
    label = "beta[0]",
    parse = TRUE,
    size = 7
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.15,
    y = three_means$svl[2],
    hjust = 0,
    label = "beta[1]",
    parse = TRUE,
    size = 7
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 3.15,
    y = three_means$svl[3] + 0.6,
    hjust = 0,
    label = "beta[2]",
    parse = TRUE,
    size = 7
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pop_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SVL (mm)")
```

## Is the categorical variable useful?

Coefficients describe relationships between levels - but is the **categorical variable as a whole** useful?

::: {.fragment}

Frame this question as:

Does a model **with** the categorical variable explain significantly more variance than a model **without** it?

:::

# Compute degrees of freedom

## Degrees of freedom are inference currency

**Data** give us information: $n$ observations

**Parameters** spend that information: $p$ coefficients

What's left over is our **degrees of freedom**

$$
df = n - p
$$

::: {.fragment}

Leftover df are what we use to estimate the noise, $\sigma$. Fewer df, less certain $\hat \sigma$, wider CIs, bigger p-values.

:::

## The information-complexity trade off

More parameters spend $df$ to improve fit.

- **Too few** parameters: the model misses real structure (underfitting)
- **Too many** parameters: the model fits the noise (overfitting)

::: {.fragment}

Every parameter has to _earn_ its df.

:::

## Example: intercept only

```{r}
null_lm <- lm(svl ~ 1, wood_frogs)
pop_only_lm <- lm(svl ~ habitat, wood_frogs)
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Rural, suburban, and urban frogs: `svl ~ 1`

$$
\begin{align}
\text{SVL} &= \beta_0 + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

- $n$ = `r nrow(wood_frogs)` frogs
- $p$ = 1 coefficient ($\beta_0$)
- $df$ = `r nrow(wood_frogs)` - 1 = `r df.residual(null_lm)`

::: {.fragment}

Residual sum of squares:

$$
\begin{align}
RSS &= \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 \\
&= `r round(rss(null_lm), 1)`
\end{align}
$$

:::

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

plot_residuals(wood_frogs, null_lm, NULL)
```

:::

:::

:::

## Example: three categories

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Same frogs: `svl ~ habitat`

$$
\begin{align}
\text{SVL} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{Habitat} = \text{Suburban}) + \beta_2 (\text{Habitat} = \text{Urban}) + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

- $n$ = `r nrow(wood_frogs)` frogs
- $p$ = 3 coefficients ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$)
- $df$ = `r nrow(wood_frogs)` - 3 = `r df.residual(pop_only_lm)`

::: {.fragment}

Residual sum of squares:

$$
\begin{align}
RSS &= \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 \\
&= `r round(rss(pop_only_lm), 1)`
\end{align}
$$

:::

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

plot_residuals(wood_frogs, pop_only_lm, NULL)
```

:::

:::

:::

## Which model is better?

| Model | $p$ | $df$ | $RSS$ |
|-------|:---:|:----:|:-----:|
| `svl ~ 1` | 1 | `r df.residual(null_lm)` | `r round(rss(null_lm), 1)` |
| `svl ~ habitat` | 3 | `r df.residual(pop_only_lm)` | `r round(rss(pop_only_lm), 1)` |

Spending 2 df on habitat cut the RSS by `r scales::percent(1 - rss(pop_only_lm) / rss(null_lm), 0.1)`.

::: {.fragment}

Was it worth it? Adding _any_ predictor reduces RSS a little, even pure noise. We need a way to say how much is _enough_.

:::

# Compare simpler and more complex models

## Cost-benefit

Adding parameters explains more, but at a cost.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Benefit**

- Smaller residuals
- More variation explained

:::

::: {.column}

**Cost**

- Spent degrees of freedom
- Less information behind each parameter

:::

:::

## Quantify the trade off: the F statistic

$$
F = \frac{(RSS_{simple} - RSS_{complex}) \ / \ (p_{complex} - p_{simple})}{RSS_{complex} \ / \ (n - p_{complex})}
$$

- **Numerator**: improvement in fit per df spent
- **Denominator**: leftover noise per df remaining

::: {.fragment}

If the extra parameters only fit noise, $F \approx 1$. Bigger $F$ means the extra parameters were worth it.

:::

## Example: intercept-only vs three categories

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center

p1 <- plot_residuals(wood_frogs, null_lm, "Simple: svl ~ 1")
p2 <- plot_residuals(wood_frogs, pop_only_lm, "Complex: svl ~ habitat")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)
```

Does habitat explain enough of the variation to justify spending 2 df?

## Intercept-only vs three categories: math

```{r}
n_three <- nrow(wood_frogs)
f_three <- ((rss(null_lm) - rss(pop_only_lm)) / 2) /
  (rss(pop_only_lm) / (n_three - 3))
p_three <- pf(f_three, 2, n_three - 3, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

$$
\begin{align}
F &= \frac{(RSS_{simple} - RSS_{complex}) \ / \ (p_{complex} - p_{simple})}{RSS_{complex} \ / \ (n - p_{complex})} \\
F &= \frac{(`r round(rss(null_lm), 1)` - `r round(rss(pop_only_lm), 1)`) \ / \ (3 - 1)}{`r round(rss(pop_only_lm), 1)` \ / \ (`r n_three` - 3)} = `r round(f_three, 2)`
\end{align}
$$

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output

anova(lm(svl ~ 1, wood_frogs), lm(svl ~ habitat, wood_frogs))
```

:::

## This has a special name: ANOVA

**AN**alysis **O**f **VA**riance. With one categorical predictor, it's _one-way_ ANOVA.

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output

anova(lm(svl ~ habitat, wood_frogs))
```

:::

- **habitat** row: the effect of the `habitat` categorical variable.
- **Residuals** row: the remaining variation in the residuals.

## Where does the p-value come from?

If $H_0$ is true (all habitat means are equal), $F$ follows an **F distribution** with $(p_{complex} - p_{simple}, \ n - p_{complex})$ df.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

f_dist <- tibble(f = seq(0, max(6, f_three + 2), by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = df(f, 2, n_three - 3))

ggplot(f_dist, aes(f, density)) +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(f_dist, f >= f_three),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = f_three, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = f_three + 0.2,
    y = 0.8,
    label = "Observed F",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 6
  ) +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("F (2, %d df)", n_three - 3),
    y = NULL,
    title = sprintf("p = %.4f", p_three)
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

Only the right tail counts: extra parameters can only _reduce_ RSS.

## Interpret the ANOVA

$H_0$: $\mu_{rural} = \mu_{suburban} = \mu_{urban}$

$H_A$: at least one habitat mean differs

::: {.fragment}

_If_ habitat had no relationship with size, we'd see an F at least this large in `r scales::percent(p_three, 0.1)` of samples. `r if (p_three < 0.05) "Reject" else "Fail to reject"` $H_0$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

But we pooled frogs of all ages, and frogs keep growing as they age. Age differences are hiding in the residuals, inflating the denominator of $F$. Could accounting for age change the answer? You'll find out in lab.

:::

# Recap

## Recap

More data means more information (df) to spend on inference.

What do we spend it on? Parameters.

More complex models explain more variation, but do they explain _enough_ variation to justify their costs? The **F statistic** answers that.

::: {.fragment}

ANOVA isn't a separate tool from linear models. It's a comparison between two linear models.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**In lab**: Does habitat matter once we account for age?

:::

## References

Jennette, M. A., Snodgrass, J. W., & Forester, D. C. (2019). Variation in age, body size, and reproductive traits among urban and rural amphibian populations. _Urban Ecosystems_, 22, 137–147. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11252-018-0801-7>

Whitehurst, M. (2021). Life in Urban Environments: The Impact of Urbanization on Life-History Traits in Amphibian Species. _QUBES Educational Resources_. <https://doi.org/10.25334/872X-7X06> (CC BY-SA 4.0)
